newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Move to create EU-wide pension funds suffers setback.
newsitem.headline: Move to create EU-wide pension funds suffers setback.

text.p: The European Commission and the $1.3-trillion European pension fund industry suffered a setback on Thursday as a European Court advocate-general said that 1994 rules advocating an EU-wide market for funds were illegal.

Advocate-General Giuseppe Tesauro has concluded that a Commission communication published in December 1994, after it failed to persuade EU finance ministers to agree on the free investment and management of funds, should be annulled.
His opinion is not binding and a final decision rests with the European Court of Justice.
Central to Tesauro's conclusions was the view that the Commission was trying to force the rules on EU governments.

"We are forced to notice that the communication on pension funds is aimed at producing a proper legal effect. (...) this consideration is sufficient to lead to the conclusion that the communication should be annulled," Tesauro said.
The Commission's controversial text threatened to challenge any national restrictions on pension fund investments which could not be justified by prudential rules.
It particularly warned EU capitals not to require fund managers to hold more than 60 percent of a fund's in instruments denominated in their own currencies.
Tesauro's opinion is a victory for France which challenged the Commission's move with the support of Spain, EU sources said.

But the European Federation for Retirement Provisions (EFRP) was optimistic that this would not slow the pace towards the development of the industry, including in countries such as France, Spain, Italy and Germany which have opposed privately run pension schemes.
EFRP represents all pension funds in the EU.
"The pressure for changes is so enormous...I think the attitude of France is no longer the same," EFRP secretary- general, Koen de Ryck, told Reuters.
France's National Assembly adopted a bill on Wednesday to allow creation of private pension funds despite long-standing trade union opposition.
Like other EU countries, the French government is faced with the fact that state-backed retirement benefit systems are no longer sufficient to finance pensions due to an ageing population.

Britain, Ireland and the Netherlands are the only countries which backed a 1991 Commission draft directive which would have done away, at least partly, with investment restrictions such as minimum requirements to invest in local securities.
The Commission believes that such restrictions are mostly intended to maintain captive markets for government bonds and to support weaker currencies.
